claim: Placoderms are the earliest branching jawed vertebrates.
source: Placoderms, as the earliest branching jawed vertebrates, are crucial to understanding how the characters of crown gnathostomes comprising Chondrichthyes and Osteichthyes evolved from their stem relatives.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Crown gnathostomes comprise Chondrichthyes and Osteichthyes.
source: Placoderms, as the earliest branching jawed vertebrates, are crucial to understanding how the characters of crown gnathostomes comprising Chondrichthyes and Osteichthyes evolved from their stem relatives.
evidence: This is stated as established taxonomic knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The dermal scales of placoderms are predominantly known from isolated material.
source: Despite the growing knowledge of the anatomy and diversity of placoderms over the past decade, the dermal scales of placoderms are predominantly known from isolated material, either morphologically or histologically, resulting in their squamation being poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Antiarcha is a clade at the root of jawed vertebrates.
source: Here we provide a comprehensive description of the squamation and scale morphology of a primitive taxon of Antiarcha (a clade at the root of jawed vertebrates), Parayunnanolepis xitunensis, based on the virtual restoration of an articulated specimen by using X-ray computed tomography.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic context.

claim: Thirteen morphotypes of scales are classified in Parayunnanolepis xitunensis.
source: Thirteen morphotypes of scales are classified to exhibit how the morphology changes with their position on the body in primitive antiarchs, based on which nine areas of the post-thoracic body are distinguished to show their scale variations in the dorsal, flank, ventral, and caudal lobe regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and detailed in the Results section.

claim: Nine areas of the post-thoracic body are distinguished in Parayunnanolepis xitunensis based on scale variations.
source: Thirteen morphotypes of scales are classified to exhibit how the morphology changes with their position on the body in primitive antiarchs, based on which nine areas of the post-thoracic body are distinguished to show their scale variations in the dorsal, flank, ventral, and caudal lobe regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and detailed in the Results section.

claim: The histological structure of yunnanolepidoid scales is described for the first time.
source: In this study, the histological structure of yunnanolepidoid scales is described for the first time based on disarticulated scales from the type locality and horizon of P. xitunensis.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution in the abstract.

claim: Yunnanolepidoid scales lack a well-developed middle layer.
source: The results demonstrate that yunnanolepidoid scales are remarkably different from their dermal plates as well as euantiarch scales in lack of a well-developed middle layer.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by histological data in the Results section.

claim: Yunnanolepidoid scales differ from their dermal plates in histological structure.
source: The results demonstrate that yunnanolepidoid scales are remarkably different from their dermal plates as well as euantiarch scales in lack of a well-developed middle layer.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by histological data.

claim: Yunnanolepidoid scales differ from euantiarch scales in histological structure.
source: The results demonstrate that yunnanolepidoid scales are remarkably different from their dermal plates as well as euantiarch scales in lack of a well-developed middle layer.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by histological data.

claim: High regionalization of squamation might be plesiomorphic for antiarchs.
source: Together, our study reveals that the high regionalization of squamation and the bipartite histological structure of scales might be plesiomorphic for antiarchs, and jawed vertebrates in general.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on comparative analysis.

claim: Jawed vertebrates possess a fully mineralized dermal skeleton that falls into two categories: macromery (large bony plates) and micromery (small scales).
source: Jawed vertebrates possess a fully mineralized dermal skeleton that falls into two categories: macromery (large bony plates) and micromery (small scales), with the latter differentiating as a squamation across the animal (Janvier, 1996; Jerve et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Squamation is a highly complex integument that varies both interspecifically and intraspecifically.
source: The squamation is a highly complex integument that varies both interspecifically and intraspecifically (Reif, 1985), and may correspond with ecology or lifestyle as well as the body plan (Ferrón and Botella, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Squamation may correspond with ecology or lifestyle as well as the body plan.
source: The squamation is a highly complex integument that varies both interspecifically and intraspecifically (Reif, 1985), and may correspond with ecology or lifestyle as well as the body plan (Ferrón and Botella, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Squamation contributes to morphological data that have been used to resolve the interrelationships of early jawed vertebrates.
source: It also contributes to morphological data that have been used to resolve the interrelationships of early jawed vertebrates (Choo et al., 2017; Qiao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Placoderms constitute the crownward part of the stem gnathostomes.
source: Placoderms constitute the crownward part of the stem gnathostomes (Dupret et al., 2014; Qiao et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Placoderms primitively bear extensive dermoskeleton.
source: They primitively bear extensive dermoskeleton (Giles et al., 2013), but appear to have recurrently reduced or lost the dermal scales in later species including many advanced arthrodires, euantiarchs, and ptyctodonts (Denison, 1978; Janvier, 1996).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Placoderms appear to have recurrently reduced or lost the dermal scales in later species including many advanced arthrodires, euantiarchs, and ptyctodonts.
source: They primitively bear extensive dermoskeleton (Giles et al., 2013), but appear to have recurrently reduced or lost the dermal scales in later species including many advanced arthrodires, euantiarchs, and ptyctodonts (Denison, 1978; Janvier, 1996).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The squamation in placoderms has only been preserved in situ in a few examples.
source: Since the squamation in placoderms has only been preserved in situ in a few examples (Goujet, 1973; Gross, 1963; Hemmings, 1978; Ivanov et al., 1996; Long and Werdelin, 1986; Lyarskaya, 1977; Stensiö, 1969; Upeniece and Upenieks, 1992), the large number of isolated placoderm scales are of uncertain affinity, and little is known about the complexity of the placoderm squamation.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Little is known about the complexity of the placoderm squamation.
source: Since the squamation in placoderms has only been preserved in situ in a few examples (Goujet, 1973; Gross, 1963; Hemmings, 1978; Ivanov et al., 1996; Long and Werdelin, 1986; Lyarskaya, 1977; Stensiö, 1969; Upeniece and Upenieks, 1992), the large number of isolated placoderm scales are of uncertain affinity, and little is known about the complexity of the placoderm squamation.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: Gnathal plates and different categories of the dermoskeleton including scales, dermal bony plates, and fin spines have been extensively studied in placoderms.

evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The histology of yunnanolepidoids is poorly known, especially for the scales.

source: Parayunnanolepis xitunensis from the Lower Devonian of South China, is known for the most complete preserved yunnanolepidoid fossil (Figure 1A–C).

claim: The scales of P. xitunensis are packed into oblique dorsoventral rows (flank scales), longitudinal files (dorsal and ventral scales), and curved linear rows (caudal lobe scales).

claim: The squamation of P. xitunensis can be divided into four large regions (dorsal, ventral, flank, and caudal lobe regions).

claim: The squamation of P. xitunensis can be further divided into nine areas.

claim: The dorsal region of P. xitunensis comprises the predorsal, dorsal fin, posterodorsal, and dorsolateral areas.

claim: Three specialized dorsal ridge scales lie in sequence just behind the ads but in front of the dorsal fin in P. xitunensis.
source: Three specialized dorsal ridge scales (Morphotype 2) lie in sequence just behind the ads (Morphotype 1) but in front of the dorsal fin.

claim: The first two dorsal ridge scales of P. xitunensis are separated by a pair of adls.

evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section.

claim: The dorsal fin area of P. xitunensis is completely covered by numerous imbricating scales.
source: The dorsal fin area is completely covered by numerous imbricating scales (Morphotype 4) (Figure 3G, H), a feature also known in other placoderms with heavy scale cover.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: Complete scale cover of the dorsal fin area is a feature also known in other placoderms with heavy scale cover.
source: The dorsal fin area is completely covered by numerous imbricating scales (Morphotype 4) (Figure 3G, H), a feature also known in other placoderms with heavy scale cover.
evidence: This is stated as comparative knowledge.

claim: Two files of flat fulcral scales are positioned just behind the dorsal fin in the posterodorsal area of P. xitunensis.
source: In the posterodorsal area, two files of flat fulcral scales (Morphotype 5) are positioned just behind the dorsal fin.

claim: The main lateral line is discernible as an open groove running around or through the crowns of the Morphotype 6–7 scales in the dorsolateral area of P. xitunensis.

evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section.

claim: The flank region of P. xitunensis comprises the anterior and posterior flank areas.
source: The flank region comprises the anterior and posterior flank areas, which are covered by anterodorsally inclined (c.40–50°) rows of scales (Morphotypes 8–9), with a different row number on either side of the body (Figure 4A, B).

claim: The flank region of P. xitunensis is covered by anterodorsally inclined (c.40–50°) rows of scales.
source: The flank region comprises the anterior and posterior flank areas, which are covered by anterodorsally inclined (c.40–50°) rows of scales (Morphotypes 8–9), with a different row number on either side of the body (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: There is a different row number on either side of the body in the flank region of P. xitunensis.
source: The flank region comprises the anterior and posterior flank areas, which are covered by anterodorsally inclined (c.40–50°) rows of scales (Morphotypes 8–9), with a different row number on either side of the body (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: The disparity of row number in the flank region might belong to abnormal arrangement of scales caused by suffering trauma.

evidence: This is an inference with a citation.

claim: The main lateral line in the dorsolateral area extends anteriorly onto the Morphotype 8 scales of the anterior flank area in P. xitunensis.
source: The main lateral line in the dorsolateral area extends anteriorly onto the Morphotype 8 scales of the anterior flank area.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section.

claim: A small pore opens onto the crown surface in some flank scales of P. xitunensis.
source: A small pore opens onto the crown surface in some flank scales (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, L).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: The squamation in the flank region of P. xitunensis exhibits a backward gradation of scales in shape (from oval, to rhombic or rectangular), thickness (from high to low crown), and size (from small to large in overall).
source: Remarkably, the squamation in the flank region exhibits a backward gradation of scales in shape (from oval, to rhombic or rectangular), thickness (from high to low crown), and size (from small to large in overall) (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: The size increase from anterior to posterior in P. xitunensis might indicate the pfs developed earlier than more anterior ones.
source: The size increase from anterior to posterior, might indicate the pfs developed earlier than more anterior ones.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed data.

claim: The size gradation in P. xitunensis is contrary to that in many other early vertebrates, such as Tremataspis, Guiyu, Mimipiscis, and Gogosardina.
source: However, this size gradation is contrary to that in many other early vertebrates, such as Tremataspis (Märss et al., 2015), Guiyu (Cui et al., 2019), Mimipiscis (Choo, 2012), and Gogosardina (Choo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparative statement with citations.

claim: The ventral region of P. xitunensis comprises the ventral and ventrolateral areas.
source: The ventral region comprises the ventral and ventrolateral areas.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section.

claim: The scales in the ventral region of P. xitunensis are flatter than those in other areas.
source: The scales in the ventral region are flatter than those in other areas.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section.

claim: A file of ventral scutes covering the ventral area of P. xitunensis is flanked by a file of ventrolateral scales in the ventrolateral area.
source: A file of ventral scutes (Morphotype 10–11) covering the ventral area, is flanked by a file of ventrolateral scales (Morphotype 12) in the ventrolateral area.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section.

claim: The squamation in the ventral region of P. xitunensis exhibits a backward gradation of scales in shape (from pentagonal to rhombic), size (from large to small), the development of lateral lamina (from well to weakly developed) and overlapping degree (from heavily to slightly overlapped).
source: The squamation in the ventral region also exhibits a backward gradation of scales in shape (from pentagonal to rhombic), size (from large to small), the development of lateral lamina (from well to weakly developed) and overlapping degree (from heavily to slightly overlapped) (Figure 5A, D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: A few additional scales are interspersed between the regularly arranged ventral scutes and flank scales in P. xitunensis.
source: A few additional scales are interspersed between the regularly arranged ventral scutes and flank scales (Figure 5D, L, is), and resembling the surrounding scales in morphotypes.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: The same condition of interspersed scales was also found in the squamation of Asterolepis.
source: The same condition was also found in the squamation of Asterolepis (Ivanov et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a comparative statement with a citation.

claim: The caudal lobe region of P. xitunensis is covered by tiny scales (Morphotype 13).
source: The caudal lobe region, or the ventral lobe of the caudal peduncle, is covered by tiny scales (Morphotype 13).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section.

claim: Morphotype 13 scales are the smallest amongst the squamation of P. xitunensis.
source: Being the smallest amongst the squamation (Figure 6B), these scales are arranged in linear rows as the tail scales of other antiarchs, such as Pterichthyodes (Hemmings, 1978).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: Morphotype 13 scales are arranged in linear rows as the tail scales of other antiarchs, such as Pterichthyodes.
source: Being the smallest amongst the squamation (Figure 6B), these scales are arranged in linear rows as the tail scales of other antiarchs, such as Pterichthyodes (Hemmings, 1978).
evidence: This is a comparative statement with a citation.

claim: Yunnanolepidoid antiarchs display abundant fossil records in the Early Devonian sediments of South China.
source: Despite yunnanolepidoid antiarchs displaying abundant fossil records in the Early Devonian sediments of South China (Burrow et al., 2000; Zhao and Zhu, 2010; Zhu, 1996; Zhu et al., 2000), the identification of isolated scales has proven difficult as the scale sculpture, mainly composed of round tubercles, is less diagnostic.

claim: The identification of isolated yunnanolepidoid scales has proven difficult as the scale sculpture, mainly composed of round tubercles, is less diagnostic.
source: Despite yunnanolepidoid antiarchs displaying abundant fossil records in the Early Devonian sediments of South China (Burrow et al., 2000; Zhao and Zhu, 2010; Zhu, 1996; Zhu et al., 2000), the identification of isolated scales has proven difficult as the scale sculpture, mainly composed of round tubercles, is less diagnostic.
evidence: This is stated as a challenge in the field.

claim: Yunnanolepidoid scales have never been investigated histologically prior to this study.
source: As such, yunnanolepidoid scales have never been investigated histologically.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Isolated scales from the type locality and horizon of P. xitunensis can be assigned to yunnanolepidoids with a reference to the articulated specimen of P. xitunensis.
source: These isolated scales (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) are difficult to be referred to as any definite species, however, they can be assigned to yunnanolepidoids with a reference to the articulated specimen of P. xitunensis described here in detail.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological approach.

claim: The yunnanolepidoid scale uniformly comprises two main divisions: a compact superficial layer, and a thick, lamellar basal layer.
source: The thin sections through different morphotypes of yunnanolepidoid scales show that the scale uniformly comprises two main divisions: a compact superficial layer, and a thick, lamellar basal layer (sup, bas; Figure 7).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: The histology of yunnanolepidoid scales is remarkably different from that of their dermal bony plates, which exhibits a three-layered structure including a thick cancellous spongiosa in the middle.
source: Thus, the histology of yunnanolepidoid scales is remarkably different from that of their dermal bony plates, which exhibits a three-layered structure including a thick cancellous spongiosa in the middle as in Yunnanolepis and Chuchinolepis (Giles et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section with a citation.

claim: The dermal skeletal differentiation across the dermal shield and scales with respect to the middle layer is also the case for heterostracans and osteostracans.
source: Significantly, the dermal skeletal differentiation across the dermal shield and scales with respect to the middle layer, is also the case for heterostracans and osteostracans (Denison, 1947; O'Shea et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparative statement with citations.

claim: The superficial layer of the yunnanolepidoid scale is confined to the tubercular ornament.
source: The superficial layer of the yunnanolepidoid scale is confined to the tubercular ornament.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section.

claim: No apparent dentine tubules could be identified in yunnanolepidoid scales due to recrystallization of mineralized tissues.
source: No apparent dentine tubules could be identified due to recrystallization (rt; Figure 7E) of mineralized tissues.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: Dentine tissue was reported in yunnanolepidoid dermal plates.
source: However, the dentine tissue was reported in yunnanolepidoid dermal plates (Giles et al., 2013; Young, 2008), suggesting another potential differentiation across the scale and the dermal plate.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The absence of dentine tubules in yunnanolepidoid scales suggests another potential differentiation across the scale and the dermal plate.
source: However, the dentine tissue was reported in yunnanolepidoid dermal plates (Giles et al., 2013; Young, 2008), suggesting another potential differentiation across the scale and the dermal plate.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed data and cited literature.

claim: The odontodes in the superficial layer of yunnanolepidoid scales display signs of superpositional stacking of at least three generations.
source: The odontodes in the superficial layer display signs of superpositional stacking of at least three generations (go1–3; Figure 7A), and the number of superimposed layers of odontodes decreases from the center of the scale to the edge.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: The number of superimposed layers of odontodes decreases from the center of the scale to the edge in yunnanolepidoid scales.
source: The odontodes in the superficial layer display signs of superpositional stacking of at least three generations (go1–3; Figure 7A), and the number of superimposed layers of odontodes decreases from the center of the scale to the edge.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: The younger odontodes cover the older generations of odontodes either completely or incompletely in yunnanolepidoid scales, suggesting a combined areo-superpositional growth or a compound growth pattern.
source: The younger odontodes cover the older generations of odontodes either completely or incompletely, suggesting a combined areo-superpositional growth (Ørvig, 1968) or a compound growth (Cui et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference from the observed data with citations.

claim: Polyodontode and the compound growth pattern have been considered to be plesiomorphic in jawed vertebrates.
source: Polyodontode and the compound growth pattern have been considered to be plesiomorphic in jawed vertebrates (Cui et al., 2021; Qu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The conditions in yunnanolepidoid scales offer support for the hypothesis that polyodontode and the compound growth pattern are plesiomorphic in jawed vertebrates.
source: The conditions in yunnanolepidoid scales offer support for these hypotheses.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed data.

claim: Most of the lacunae in yunnanolepidoid scales are star-shaped with rounded or more elongated cell bodies.
source: Most of the lacunae are star-shaped with rounded or more elongated cell bodies (lac; Figure 7A), and have ramifying canaliculi in all directions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: The lacunae in yunnanolepidoid scales have ramifying canaliculi in all directions.
source: Most of the lacunae are star-shaped with rounded or more elongated cell bodies (lac; Figure 7A), and have ramifying canaliculi in all directions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: The vasculature in yunnanolepidoid scales might be supplied by occasional ascending canals from the basal layer, which opened to the surface but was buried later by younger odontodes.
source: The vasculature might be supplied by occasional ascending canals (vc; Figure 7A) from the basal layer, which opened to the surface but was buried later by younger odontodes.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed data with reference to figures.

claim: The middle/spongiosa layer may be poorly developed or absent in certain morphotypes of yunnanolepidoid scales.
source: In this case, the middle/spongiosa layer may be poorly developed or absent in certain morphotypes.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed data.

claim: The basal layer of yunnanolepidoid scales is permeated by vertical Sharpey's fibers.
source: The basal layer is permeated by vertical Sharpey's fibers (sf; Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: The Sharpey's fibers in yunnanolepidoid scales converge towards the center of the scale, at right angles to the lines of the laminae.
source: These fibers converge towards the center of the scale, at right angles to the lines of the laminae.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section.

claim: The scale base of yunnanolepidoid scales shows a series of growth lines.
source: The scale base shows a series of growth lines (gl; Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: P. xitunensis exhibits remarkable morphological variability in the scales of nine body areas.
source: As described above, P. xitunensis exhibits remarkable morphological variability in the scales of nine body areas.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Discussion section.

claim: High regionalization of squamation is present in Romundina and Radotina, two primitive members of placoderms.
source: Also present in Romundina and Radotina (Ørvig, 1975), another two primitive members of placoderms (Li et al., 2021; Vaškaninová et al., 2020), the high regionalization of squamation probably represents a primitive character for jawed vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The high regionalization of squamation probably represents a primitive character for jawed vertebrates.
source: Also present in Romundina and Radotina (Ørvig, 1975), another two primitive members of placoderms (Li et al., 2021; Vaškaninová et al., 2020), the high regionalization of squamation probably represents a primitive character for jawed vertebrates.
evidence: This is an inference from comparative data with citations.

claim: The squamation regionalization in the ventral and dorsal regions of the body is reduced in euantiarchs.
source: In comparison, the squamation regionalization in the ventral and dorsal regions of the body is reduced in euantiarchs (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a comparative statement with reference to figures.

claim: Most bothriolepidoids have almost naked bodies.
source: Most bothriolepidoids have almost naked bodies, such as Bothriolepis canadensis, in which only a small patch of square scales occurs along the lower margin of the tail (Stensiö, 1948).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Bothriolepis canadensis has only a small patch of square scales along the lower margin of the tail.
source: Most bothriolepidoids have almost naked bodies, such as Bothriolepis canadensis, in which only a small patch of square scales occurs along the lower margin of the tail (Stensiö, 1948).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: B. gippslandiensis and B. cullodenensis are exceptions among bothriolepidoids in having a complete squamation.
source: The exceptions are B. gippslandiensis and B. cullodenensis (Long, 1983; Long and Werdelin, 1986), which have a complete squamation with three regional divisions: the ventrolateral, dorsal fin, and flank areas.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: B. gippslandiensis and B. cullodenensis have a complete squamation with three regional divisions: the ventrolateral, dorsal fin, and flank areas.
source: The exceptions are B. gippslandiensis and B. cullodenensis (Long, 1983; Long and Werdelin, 1986), which have a complete squamation with three regional divisions: the ventrolateral, dorsal fin, and flank areas.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Pterichthyodes milleri appears to have the highest regional differentiation amongst asterolepidoids, with about six body areas.
source: Pterichthyodes milleri appears to have the highest regional differentiation amongst asterolepidoids, with about six body areas, that is predorsal, dorsal fin, posterodorsal, flank, ventral, and caudal lobe areas (Hemmings, 1978).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The squamation of Asterolepis can be divided into three areas: dorsal fin, dorsal, and flank areas.
source: The squamation of Asterolepis can be divided into three areas: dorsal fin, dorsal, and flank areas, based on its scale morphotypes (Ivanov et al., 1995; Ivanov et al., 1996).

source: The squamation of Remigolepis can also be divided into three areas: predorsal, posterodorsal, and flank areas (Johanson, 1997), or even fewer areas in the species from northern China (Pan et al., 1987).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The squamation is simplified in the aspect of regionalization or disparity in euantiarchs.
source: It seems that the squamation is simplified in the aspect of regionalization or disparity in euantiarchs, and further simplified in the clade comprising Asterolepis and Remigolepis, as their ventral scales are not differentiated from the flank scales (Figure 8).
evidence: This is an inference from comparative data with reference to figures.

claim: The squamation is further simplified in the clade comprising Asterolepis and Remigolepis, as their ventral scales are not differentiated from the flank scales.
source: It seems that the squamation is simplified in the aspect of regionalization or disparity in euantiarchs, and further simplified in the clade comprising Asterolepis and Remigolepis, as their ventral scales are not differentiated from the flank scales (Figure 8).
evidence: This is an inference from comparative data with reference to figures.

claim: The simplification of squamation has also occurred in crown sarcopterygians and actinopterygians.
source: The simplification of squamation has also occurred in crown sarcopterygians and actinopterygians (Cui et al., 2019; Friedman and Blom, 2006; Mondéjar-Fernández and Clément, 2012), and possibly in crown chondrichthyans (Ferrón et al., 2018), suggesting substantial parallelism of squamation in early jawed vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The simplification of squamation has possibly occurred in crown chondrichthyans.
source: The simplification of squamation has also occurred in crown sarcopterygians and actinopterygians (Cui et al., 2019; Friedman and Blom, 2006; Mondéjar-Fernández and Clément, 2012), and possibly in crown chondrichthyans (Ferrón et al., 2018), suggesting substantial parallelism of squamation in early jawed vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: There is substantial parallelism of squamation in early jawed vertebrates.
source: The simplification of squamation has also occurred in crown sarcopterygians and actinopterygians (Cui et al., 2019; Friedman and Blom, 2006; Mondéjar-Fernández and Clément, 2012), and possibly in crown chondrichthyans (Ferrón et al., 2018), suggesting substantial parallelism of squamation in early jawed vertebrates.
evidence: This is an inference from comparative data with citations.

claim: The dermal skeleton of heterostracans, osteostracans, placoderms, and early osteichthyans usually consists of three principal layers: a superficial layer composed of dentine and enameloid/enamel; a trabecular/cancellous layer composed of vascular bone; and a compact basal layer composed of lamellar/pseudolamellar bone.
source: The dermal skeleton of heterostracans, osteostracans, placoderms, and early osteichthyans usually consists of three principal layers: a superficial layer composed of dentine and enameloid/enamel; a trabecular/cancellous layer composed of vascular bone; and a compact basal layer composed of lamellar/pseudolamellar bone (Burrow and Turner, 1999; Donoghue and Sansom, 2002; Giles et al., 2013; Qu et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The tripartite structure was considered to be plesiomorphic for early jawed vertebrates.
source: This tripartite structure was considered to be plesiomorphic for early jawed vertebrates (Qu et al., 2015b; O'Shea et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Different dermal units evolve as independent modules.
source: However, different dermal units evolve as independent modules (Qu et al., 2015b), and vary in histological structure as suggested by the conditions in yunnanolepidoids.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Different dermal units vary in histological structure as suggested by the conditions in yunnanolepidoids.
source: However, different dermal units evolve as independent modules (Qu et al., 2015b), and vary in histological structure as suggested by the conditions in yunnanolepidoids.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed data with a citation.

claim: Anaspid, thelodont and galeaspid scales lack an extensive osteonal middly layer.
source: Anaspid, thelodont and galeaspid scales lack an extensive osteonal middly layer (Burrow et al., 2013; Keating and Donoghue, 2016; Wang et al., 2005).

claim: Heterostracans have body scales with poorly developed or no middle layer.
source: Heterostracans have body scales with poorly developed or no middle layer (Keating et al., 2015; Soehn and Wilson, 1990).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The middle layer with varied development conditions has been reported in tremataspid scales.

evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Ornament on the external surface of the osteostracan scales changes from smooth with pores, to variable shaped tubercles in combination with nodules, ridges, ribs, and inter-ridge grooves.
source: Ornament on the external surface of the osteostracan scales changes from smooth with pores, to variable shaped tubercles in combination with nodules, ridges, ribs, and inter-ridge grooves (Märss et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Yunnanolepidoid scales bear the round tubercle sculpture on the surface.
source: Yunnanolepidoid scales bear the round tubercle sculpture on the surface and lack the well-developed middle layer, in contrast with that of euantiarchs.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Discussion section.

claim: The middle partition of scales assigned to Asterolepis ornata coincides with the features of the middle layer, such as the 'vascular canals surrounded by osteons'.
source: The middle partition of scales assigned to Asterolepis ornata (Lyarskaya, 1977) and Wurungulepis denisoni (Burrow and Turner, 1998) coincides with the features of the middle layer, such as the 'vascular canals surrounded by osteons'.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The Remigolepis scale develops a thick middle layer bearing the upper part of the canal system.
source: The Remigolepis scale also develops a thick middle layer bearing the upper part of the canal system (Lukševičs, 1991).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The asterolepidoid scale is much more variable than that of yunnanolepidoid antiarchs in ornamentation.
source: Considering ornamentation, the asterolepidoid scale is much more variable than that of yunnanolepidoid antiarchs; its sculpture changes with the body areas longitudinally from a smooth surface to a combination of nodules, longitudinal crests/ridges, grooves, irregular tubercles, and indistinct pits (Hemmings, 1978; Ivanov et al., 1996; Young, 1990).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Only the histology of Ohioaspis scales was investigated in rhenanids.
source: In rhenanids, only the histology of Ohioaspis scales was investigated (Burrow and Turner, 1999).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The middle layer is not developed in Ohioaspis scales as the main body of vascular canals is buried within the older generations of tubercles and thus belongs to the superficial layer.
source: The middle layer is not developed as the main body of vascular canals is buried within the older generations of tubercles (Gross, 1973) and thus belongs to the superficial layer.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The scales of Ohioaspis have stellate tubercles with a multitude of ridgelets around them.
source: The scales of Ohioaspis have stellate tubercles with a multitude of ridgelets around them (Burrow and Turner, 1999; Gross, 1973), whiles the scales of Gemuendina and Jagorina are simply ornamented with round tubercles (Denison, 1978).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The scales of Gemuendina and Jagorina are simply ornamented with round tubercles.
source: The scales of Ohioaspis have stellate tubercles with a multitude of ridgelets around them (Burrow and Turner, 1999; Gross, 1973), whiles the scales of Gemuendina and Jagorina are simply ornamented with round tubercles (Denison, 1978).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The absence of the spongiosa in the scale was ever perceived as a feature for acanthothoracids.
source: The absence of the spongiosa in the scale was ever perceived as a feature for acanthothoracids (Burrow, 1996; Denison, 1978).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The middle layer is very weakly developed in scales of Jerulalepis and radotinids.
source: The middle layer is very weakly developed in scales of Jerulalepis and radotinids (Burrow, 1996; Stensiö, 1969).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Different conditions occur in the scales referred to Murrindalaspis, Connemarraspis, and Romundina, which bear a well-developed middle layer.
source: However, different conditions occur in the scales referred to Murrindalaspis, Connemarraspis, and Romundina, which bear a well-developed middle layer in addition to the complex ornamentation composed of stellate, ridged or polygonal tubercles as in the stem osteichthyan Lophosteus (Burrow, 2006; Burrow and Turner, 1998; Gross, 1969; Long and Young, 1988).
